{"id": "96:14/q01", "question": "Who is the person asked whether he knows God sees?", "turns_on": "Whether the pronoun and changing addresses are tied to the Abu Jahl incident, the Prophet and opponent in turn, or the general audience.", "positions": [{"id": "96:14/q01/p1", "position": "The forbidding man is Abu Jahl.", "reasons": "Al-Tabari and others identify the opponent who forbade Muhammad's prayer; al-Farra explicitly makes this question about Abu Jahl. Al-Alusi reports Ibn Atiyya's claim of agreement that the servant is the Messenger and the forbidder Abu Jahl. Ibn Ashur says the prior prohibition supplies the omitted referent."}, {"id": "96:14/q01/p2", "position": "The question can address Muhammad about Abu Jahl, or address Abu Jahl himself.", "reasons": "Al-Mawardi gives both possible interlocutors. Al-Alusi reports a judge-like alternation between the unbeliever and Prophet. Al-Baydawi reports a shift to the unbeliever in the second address."}, {"id": "96:14/q01/p3", "position": "It may refer to either the praying servant, who knows God sees, or the forbider, who fails to heed that knowledge.", "reasons": "Elmalili says either pronoun assignment still threatens the prohibiter."}, {"id": "96:14/q01/p4", "position": "The address extends to any capable listener, or to humanity.", "reasons": "Al-Alusi cites 96:8 for the humanity reading. Al-Razi's general reading of al-insan and Bint al-Shati's discussion extend the scene beyond its particular occasion."}]}
{"id": "96:14/q02", "question": "How does 'know' take the following bāʾ phrase?", "turns_on": "Whether the preposition follows a certainty sense of yaʿlam or is an added bāʾ before its object.", "positions": [{"id": "96:14/q02/p1", "position": "Know means be certain, accounting for the bāʾ.", "reasons": "Ibn Ashur expressly treats yaʿlam as carrying certainty."}, {"id": "96:14/q02/p2", "position": "The bāʾ is an added preposition on an object that the verb can take directly.", "reasons": "Al-Zarkashi's Burhan compares 2:195 and 19:25, and cites 22:15, 38:33, and 21:31 among parallels."}]}
{"id": "96:14/q03", "question": "How does the final question complete the preceding arāʾayta clauses and conditions?", "turns_on": "The object requirements of arāʾayta, whether the closing interrogative is an apodosis or a fresh sentence, and whether an interrogative apodosis needs fāʾ.", "positions": [{"id": "96:14/q03/p1", "position": "It is the expressed answer to the later conditional, with the earlier answer omitted or supplied by it.", "reasons": "Al-Zamakhshari allows a question to answer a conditional without fāʾ, using 6:47 and other interrogative examples; al-Radi approves. The forbidden person and conditional supply arāʾayta's objects, with the second arāʾayta emphatic. Al-Baydawi and al-Nasafi likewise supply the earlier answer from the later condition."}, {"id": "96:14/q03/p2", "position": "The final question is an independent rebuke; conditional answers are omitted and indicated by it or by arāʾayta.", "reasons": "Al-Alusi distinguishes omission from grammatical tanāzuʿ: the clauses are semantically demanded, not syntactically shared. Ibn Ashur supplies an implicit answer that God knows and punishes; the final interrogative then begins afresh. Elmalili prefers this resumed reading. Al-Zarkashi reconciles Sibawayh's required object with Quranic cases by positing a conditional pointing to an omitted object and a fresh question."}, {"id": "96:14/q03/p3", "position": "The repeated arāʾayta clauses substitute for the first; the final question is their predicate or second object.", "reasons": "Al-Akhfash makes the second arāʾayta appositional to the first. Al-Tabari treats three repetitions as substitutions. Al-Qurtubi reports the same predicate analysis. Al-Biqaʿi insists the second object is an interrogative. Al-Alusi's version places both conditionals in the first question's second-object slot and lets the final verse answer the second."}, {"id": "96:14/q03/p4", "position": "All three challenges have omitted completions, which the one concise final threat supplies.", "reasons": "Ibn Atiyya treats arāʾayta as an interrogative challenge without two cognitive objects. Its sequence gains one expansive but compressed conclusion; Abu Hayyan reports this reading."}, {"id": "96:14/q03/p5", "position": "The first arāʾayta is visual, while the later two are intellectual and take conditional material as second objects.", "reasons": "Al-Alusi reports this as one parsing, with the last condition's explicit answer and the earlier omitted one; unjoining the final clause stresses the actual event and threat."}, {"id": "96:14/q03/p6", "position": "All three arāʾaytas are intellectual; the first condition fills an object's place and the last question is independently stated.", "reasons": "Al-Alusi reports a first relative clause as object one, a conditional or its omitted answer as object two, and a third question with omitted first object. The unjoined close sharpens the real threat."}, {"id": "96:14/q03/p7", "position": "The interrogative suspends arāʾayta's government, leaving its second object unspoken and directing attention to the warning.", "reasons": "Ibn Ashur treats the intellectual verb's objects as omitted for concision, identified by the servant and prohibition. Bint al-Shati cites 107:1, 19:77, 25:43, 45:23 and 53:33 for interrogative arāʾayta omitting its second object, and argues the repeated formula needs no inferred complement or hidden conditional answer."}, {"id": "96:14/q03/p8", "position": "A conditional can occupy the second object by the combined sense of its condition and interrogative consequence.", "reasons": "Al-Khafaji's reply, also attributed to al-Radi and al-Damamini, allows literal or semantic occupation of the slot. Al-Alusi rejects a categorical interrogative-only rule as conflicting with Sibawayh's reported preference."}, {"id": "96:14/q03/p9", "position": "A conditional cannot be the required second object; an interrogative or oath clause is needed.", "reasons": "Abu Hayyan raises the grammatical objection; Bint al-Shati cites his account of frequent Quranic interrogative objects."}, {"id": "96:14/q03/p10", "position": "An interrogative apodosis lacking fāʾ is impermissible outside poetic necessity.", "reasons": "Abu Hayyan invokes grammarians' rule for request-like clauses; al-Damamini questions hal yahliku at 6:47; Ibn Ashur says most grammarians, including Zamakhshari's Mufassal, require fāʾ. Bint al-Shati objects to the extra arāʾayta as well."}, {"id": "96:14/q03/p11", "position": "The Quran also uses conditional questions followed by interrogatives without fāʾ.", "reasons": "Bint al-Shati cites 6:40, 6:46, 6:47, 28:71–72, 11:88, 41:52 and 10:50, asking readers to attend to Quranic usage beyond school grammar."}]}
{"id": "96:14/q04", "question": "Why is this knowledge framed as an interrogative rebuke?", "turns_on": "The notes give complementary explanations of the question's rebuking and astonishment effects.", "positions": [{"id": "96:14/q04/p1", "position": "The question confirms what the opponents themselves admit and exposes the contradiction of defying the Prophet under God's sight.", "reasons": "Al-Biqaʿi says the denier's conduct is irrational despite divine monitoring and control; Ibn Ashur calls the interrogative a rebuke for failing to protect himself."}, {"id": "96:14/q04/p2", "position": "The separated final clause makes each prior reproach forceful and the actual denial especially threatening.", "reasons": "Al-Alusi says the unjoined close signals the real occurrence of denial after a broadened hypothetical; three distinct reproaches concern forbidding prayer, claiming piety, then denying truth."}, {"id": "96:14/q04/p3", "position": "The unusual event is put as a question to evoke astonishment.", "reasons": "Ibn Ashur explains that an incredible known event elicits a request for confirmation and compares 88:1; al-Alusi says future wording vividly recalls the strange past scene."}, {"id": "96:14/q04/p4", "position": "The neutral 'servant' and hypothetical guidance make a fair-minded concession before judging the forbider.", "reasons": "Al-Alusi says it avoids initially naming a chosen prophet, invites any discerning hearer, and gives the forbidder's claimed guidance and piety a hearing."}]}
{"id": "96:14/q05", "question": "Whom or what does God see here?", "turns_on": "Whether the omitted object is understood from the prayer incident and the forbider's conduct, both sides' states, or all that exists.", "positions": [{"id": "96:14/q05/p1", "position": "God sees the forbidding man's acts, words and intended harm.", "reasons": "Al-Mawardi adds that God hears his words and prevents his intended harm to the Messenger. Ibn Kathir similarly joins hearing and sight. Al-Qurtubi connects sight with knowledge of Abu Jahl's conduct."}, {"id": "96:14/q05/p2", "position": "God sees the praying servant while the forbider tries to stop him.", "reasons": "Al-Mawardi presents this as another object of God's sight; one full-text note names Abu Jahl as the person praying as well as the forbider, a variant wording within that report."}, {"id": "96:14/q05/p3", "position": "God sees each person's guidance or error, and all their states.", "reasons": "Al-Kashshaf and al-Nasafi join divine observation to requital. Al-Baydawi considers both the forbider's supposed guidance and real denial; Qutb contrasts the denying opponent and guided worshipper."}, {"id": "96:14/q05/p4", "position": "The unexpressed object makes God's seeing encompass every existent.", "reasons": "Ibn Ashur explicitly says the omission generalizes the object; al-Biqaʿi calls divine sight and knowledge unrestricted over every visible and knowable thing."}]}
{"id": "96:14/q06", "question": "What does divine seeing mean?", "turns_on": "Whether 'seeing' is an irreducible divine perception or interpreted through knowledge; the notes also discuss its unlimited extent.", "positions

": [{"id": "96:14/q06/p1", "position": "God truly sees things; sight is not reduced to knowledge.", "reasons": "Al-Jishumi accepts literal divine seeing and rejects a Baghdadi claim that 'sees' only means 'knows'."}, {"id": "96:14/q06/p2", "position": "God's seeing is His perception or knowledge of deeds and perceptible things, without bodily organs or likeness to creatures.", "reasons": "Ibn Atiyya explicitly denies corporeal implication. Ibn Ashur defines it as knowledge relating to perceptible things. The Baghdadi 'means knows' view is reported by al-Jishumi, who rejects it."}, {"id": "96:14/q06/p3", "position": "God's sight and knowledge are unrestricted, grounding His power to punish wrongdoers and support the obedient.", "reasons": "Al-Biqaʿi says He knows every knowable and sees every visible thing. Al-Tabataba'i infers this from God's creating everything, a premise polytheists themselves acknowledge."}]}
{"id": "96:14/q07", "question": "What warning or lesson does God's seeing convey?", "turns_on": "The notes emphasize requital, the immediate rebuke for forfeited guidance, the denial of practical knowledge, or vigilance.", "positions": [{"id": "96:14/q07/p1", "position": "God observes the wrongdoing and will punish or fully requite it; this deters sin and encourages obedience.", "reasons": "Al-Tabari, al-Baghawi and others address Abu Jahl's forbidden prayer. Al-Razi includes resurrection and atom-small acts that escape no divine knowledge; al-Tabrisi says obedience and avoidance of sin follow. Ibn Ashur calls seeing a metonym for punishment. Al-Biqaʿi pairs punishment of misguiders with aid to the obedient."}, {"id": "96:14/q07/p2", "position": "The verse is an immediate rebuke and threat to a man whose denial and turning away cost him guidance.", "reasons": "Al-Farra contrasts the guided praying servant and the denying forbider. Al-Alusi reports Isam al-Din's account of missed high rank, acquired harm and distance from God; he distances himself from that elaboration. Al-Razi's reported hypothetical asks what a sensible, wealthy man should have chosen."}, {"id": "96:14/q07/p3", "position": "The final question says Abu Jahl does not actually know or heed that God sees.", "reasons": "Al-Baghawi reads the following kalla as denying the knowledge presupposed in the rebuke."}, {"id": "96:14/q07/p4", "position": "Knowing that God sees should produce vigilant self-observation on the way to direct witnessing.", "reasons": "Al-Qushayri says a person lacking vigilance cannot advance to witnessing."}]}
{"id": "96:14/q08", "question": "How broadly does the warning apply to forbidding worship?", "turns_on": "Whether a restriction targets worship itself or a separate wrong or protected interest, and how far the specific occasion generalizes.", "positions": [{"id": "96:14/q08/p1", "position": "It applies beyond Abu Jahl to anyone who obstructs prayer or other obedience, including distraction from worship.", "reasons": "Al-Razi extends the threat to everyone preventing obedience; al-Alusi extends it to verbal or practical prevention of other worship. Bint al-Shati says a specific occasion does not confine general wording. Kur'an Yolu prefers a universal application to tyrants obstructing religion's goodness, truth and justice."}, {"id": "96:14/q08/p2", "position": "Preventing prayer in a usurped place or disliked time is outside this warning because the objection is to an accompanying wrong.", "reasons": "Al-Razi and al-Alusi distinguish forbidding the transgression from forbidding prayer itself."}, {"id": "96:14/q08/p3", "position": "A master or husband may limit voluntary worship for a protected interest, with God's permission.", "reasons": "Al-Razi gives a slave's night prayer or voluntary fast and a wife's retreat as examples; the aim is welfare, not hostility to worship."}, {"id": "96:14/q08/p4", "position": "One should avoid explicitly prohibiting a worshipper's prayer when possible.", "reasons": "Al-Alusi reports Ali's fear of this threat when people prayed before Eid: he stated what he saw the Prophet do. Abu Hanifa likewise answered Abu Yusuf with the proper formula and prostration rather than an explicit ban."}]}
{"id": "96:14/q09", "question": "What happened when the opponent tried to stop the Prophet praying?", "turns_on": "The transmitted accounts differ on names, manner of prevention and the prayer scene; chronology is used to test the Abu Talib story.", "positions": [{"id": "96:14/q09/p1", "position": "Abu Jahl threatened to trample the Prophet but recoiled from a trench of fire, terror and wings.", "reasons": "Abu Hurayra's report includes his oath by al-Lat and al-Uzza; the Prophet said angels would seize him limb by limb. Al-Baghawi's version is uncertain whether the revelation clause belongs to Abu Hurayra's narration or elsewhere; al-Alusi says the passage through the sura was then revealed."}, {"id": "96:14/q09/p2", "position": "Abu Jahl came on the Prophet praying and forbade him; he also verbally repeated his prohibition.", "reasons": "Ibn Abbas ties the incident to the passage through the lying forelock. Al-Alusi says al-Tirmidhi authenticated the verbal warning, also transmitted by Ahmad and others; Qatada says the passage concerned the threatened trampling."}, {"id": "96:14/q09/p3", "position": "The forbider was Umayya ibn Khalaf, who stopped Salman from praying.", "reasons": "Al-Hasan supplies the names; al-Alusi deems it unlikely because Salman converted in Medina while the sura is Meccan, though he says the general warning would cover Umayya if true."}, {"id": "96:14/q09/p4", "position": "The prayer was Zuhr, also reported as the first congregational prayer with the Prophet, Abu Bakr and Ali.", "reasons": "Al-Alusi attributes these scene details to Abu Hayyan."}, {"id": "96:14/q09/p5", "position": "Abu Talib brought Ja'far to pray beside the Prophet and praised and protected him.", "reasons": "Al-Alusi reports Abu Hayyan's story, then questions it: the Mi'raj and obligatory prayer are dated after Abu Talib's death by Ibn Hazm, Ibn Faris and al-Suddi, at one year, fifteen months and seventeen months before Hijra respectively. A competing al-Zuhri chronology puts the Mi'raj five years after the mission, favored by Nawawi and Qurtubi, with objections noted."}, {"id": "96:14/q09/p6", "position": "The forbidding may have been physical prevention, revealing the tyrant's limited power.", "reasons": "Al-Alusi reports this explanation of the wording."}]}
{"id": "96:14/q10", "question": "How does this verse close the sequence about forbidding prayer?", "turns_on": "Who is the subject of the guidance hypothetical, whether its positive case is genuine or sarcastic, and how the successive challenges culminate here.", "positions": [{"id": "96:14/q10/p1", "position": "It closes three rising reproaches: forbidding prayer, claiming guidance while forbidding it, and actually denying and turning away.", "reasons": "Al-Alusi treats each as independently threatened; the majority instead treats the first conditional as sarcastic concession of the forbider's claimed guidance in idolatry and the second as his evident denial. Prayer's enacted example is stronger than speech, and forbidding it implies commanding its opposite."}, {"id": "96:14/q10/p2", "position": "It contrasts a guided praying servant who calls to piety with the forbider who denies and turns away.", "reasons": "Al-Farra shifts the first condition's pronouns to the servant and the later verbs and knowing to the forbider; the omitted result is astonishment. The connective aw can divide or mean and. Abu Hayyan adds that prayer reforms the Prophet and calling to piety reforms others, both provoking Abu Jahl."}, {"id": "96:14/q10/p3", "position": "Both conditions concern the forbider: a supposedly good course is impossible, while his actual denial independently brings the threat.", "reasons": "Al-Baydawi and al-Nasafi present his supposed idol-guidance versus rejection of truth; Bursevi says the first supposition broadens the case and the second independently triggers punishment. Al-Alusi reports the majority's sarcastic reading."}, {"id": "96:14/q10/p4", "position": "The sequence laments a self-sufficient tyrant's missed guidance and earned punishment before this final threat.", "reasons": "Isam al-Din says 96:9 exposes tyranny, 96:11–12 lost benefit and 96:13 acquired harm; al-Alusi declines to adopt his elaboration. The Imam's reported alternative asks what a rational wealthy man should choose and laments higher ranks forfeited."}, {"id": "96:14/q10/p5", "position": "The warning completes the earlier challenge in one concise threat suited to each formulation.", "reasons": "Ibn Atiyya says the earlier questions have broad omitted completions and one close suffices; Abu Hayyan relays this."}, {"id": "96:14/q10/p6", "position": "The sequence was placed after earlier revealed opening verses when public preaching and prayer later provoked Abu Jahl.", "reasons": "Bint al-Shati reports al-Razi's first solution that the rest of the sura was revealed later and directed to be placed at the start; she finds a later public-prayer setting plausible. She also reports his generic reading of humanity and leaves both possible."}]}
{"id": "96:14/q11", "question": "What other textual and transmission notes bear on this verse or its sura?", "turns_on": "Different Mi'raj chronologies are reported; the other notes concern a sura virtue and an editorial cross-reference.", "positions": [{"id": "96:14/q11/p1", "position": "The Mi'raj and obligation of prayer are dated late enough to challenge the Abu Talib story.", "reasons": "Al-Alusi cites Ibn Hazm's one year, Ibn Faris's one year and three months, and al-Suddi's one year and five months before Hijra, all after Abu Talib's death."}, {"id": "96:14/q11/p2", "position": "Another Mi'raj chronology places it five years after the prophetic commission.", "reasons": "Al-Alusi reports Qadi Iyad's report from al-Zuhri, favored by

Nawawi and Qurtubi, while noting objections."}, {"id": "96:14/q11/p3", "position": "A report promises the reciter the reward of reading all shorter suras.", "reasons": "Al-Baydawi Full attributes the promise to the Prophet."}, {"id": "96:14/q11/p4", "position": "A separate note directs readers to the treatment of the divine name Allah at 95:8.", "reasons": "Corpus Coranicum offers this cross-reference without an independent explanation here."}]}
{"id": "96:14/q12", "question": "What inward meaning is drawn from God's sight?", "turns_on": "The two inward notes offer different complementary contemplative points.", "positions": [{"id": "96:14/q12/p1", "position": "Nothing is beyond God, while He is behind every beyond.", "reasons": "Al-Tustari states this as the verse's inward observation."}, {"id": "96:14/q12/p2", "position": "Awareness that God sees calls for vigilance before direct witnessing.", "reasons": "Al-Qushayri makes vigilance a prerequisite to witnessing."}]}
{"id": "96:14/q13", "question": "What does the earlier arāʾayta mean in leading to this question?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "96:14/q13/p1", "position": "It means 'tell me': a request to see is used for a request to be informed.", "reasons": "Al-Alusi derives the usage from seeing's leading to knowledge and notes disagreement over whether it applies to visual and intellectual seeing alike."}]}
{"id": "96:14/q14", "question": "What wrongdoing sets up the final rebuke?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "96:14/q14/p1", "position": "Abu Jahl denies God's Book, turns from belief and prevents the Prophet's prayer, an act of human tyranny.", "reasons": "Al-Qurtubi names denial and turning away; al-Alusi describes the passage from 96:9 as consequences of human tyranny and a threat to the prayer's obstructer."}]}
{"id": "96:14/q15", "question": "How does calling the worshipper a servant sharpen the rebuke?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "96:14/q15/p1", "position": "The indefinite 'servant' may be generic, or may magnify the Prophet and increase astonishment that he is forbidden.", "reasons": "Al-Alusi reports both functions of the indefinite expression."}]}
{"id": "96:15/q01", "question": "What does kallā say here?", "turns_on": "The notes differ over whether kallā directly rebukes conduct, declares ignorance of divine sight, or reverses Abū Jahl's boast.", "positions": [{"id": "96:15/q01/p1", "position": "It rebukes and restrains the man who forbids worship.", "reasons": "Al-Ṭabarī says it denies Abū Jahl's boast that he can trample Muḥammad's neck; al-Kashshāf, al-Nasafī and al-Rāzī connect it to forbidding God's worship and commanding al-Lāt or idols. Abū Ḥayyān extends the rebuke to similar preventers; al-Biqāʿī calls the offender's blindness chosen, and Quṭb calls this the passage's decisive threat against tyranny."}, {"id": "96:15/q01/p2", "position": "It means that he does not know that God sees him.", "reasons": "Muqātil's gloss is transmitted by al-Wāḥidī and al-Rāzī; al-Rāzī adds that knowledge without acting on it counts as ignorance. Al-Baghawī and al-Ṭabrisī give the same sense."}, {"id": "96:15/q01/p3", "position": "It denies that Abū Jahl can kill or trample Muḥammad; a follower of Muḥammad will instead kill him and trample his chest.", "reasons": "Al-Rāzī gives this as an alternative answer to Abū Jahl's boast."}]}
{"id": "96:15/q02", "question": "Why is kallā placed here?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "96:15/q02/p1", "position": "This later kallā reinforces an earlier rebuke; its placement resolves suspense created by the earlier one.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿĀshūr says the closing position is the natural place for this counterpart; Corpus Coranicum observes that kallā also opens the rebuke in 96:6–8 and the final call in 96:19."}]}
{"id": "96:15/q03", "question": "What must the offender stop?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "96:15/q03/p1", "position": "He must stop forbidding prayer, denying, insulting, opposing or harming Muḥammad.", "reasons": "Muqātil names denial and turning away; al-Wāḥidī adds insult and harm; al-Biqāʿī says the conditional leaves room for stopping and repentance while preserving responsibility. Bursevī specifies repentance and submission before death. Al-Ṭabarī links the repeated 'Have you seen?' clauses in 96:9,11,13 to the same forbider who denies and turns away."}]}
{"id": "96:15/q04", "question": "How does the oath and condition work?", "turns_on": "The disagreement concerns the function of the lām before in.", "positions": [{"id": "96:15/q04/p1", "position": "The lām in la-in signals an implied oath; la-nasfaʿan answers it, supplying the omitted answer to the condition.", "reasons": "Al-Zarkashī calls the lām preparatory to the oath's answer and compares 59:12 and 3:12; al-Wāḥidī calls it an oath lām and notes that an initial lām attaches only to a noun or noun-like form. Ibn ʿĀshūr states that the condition's own apodosis is omitted; the light emphatic nūn commonly follows affirmative oaths."}, {"id": "96:15/q04/p2", "position": "The lām is simply an emphatic lām.", "reasons": "Athīr al-Dīn gives this analysis; al-Zarkashī rejects it in favor of an oath introduction."}]}
{"id": "96:15/q05", "question": "Why does yantahi lack its final yāʾ?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "96:15/q05/p1", "position": "The jussive drops the yāʾ.", "reasons": "Al-Naḥḥās says the noncanonical retained-yāʾ form assumes that yāʾ is mobile."}]}
{"id": "96:15/q06", "question": "What does nasfaʿ mean?", "turns_on": "Arabic usage cited for seizure and pulling, burning and darkening, striking, branding, or humiliation; some commentators combine these effects.", "positions": [{"id": "96:15/q06/p1", "position": "To seize, grasp and pull forcefully.", "reasons": "Abū ʿUbayda and Ibn Qutayba compare taking someone by the hand; Muʾarrij calls it Qurashī usage. Al-Mubarrad stresses a painful tug, and al-Farrāʾ includes crushing or bending the forelock. Al-Azharī, ʿAmr ibn Maʿdīkarib and other cited poets describe grabbing a horse or man's forelock. Ibn ʿAbbās, ʿIkrima and al-Ḥasan gloss it as taking hold; 55:41 supplies a Qurʾānic parallel. Al-Biqāʿī gathers dragging, pushing and striking in the violent act; Bint al-Shāṭiʾ notes the verb occurs only here in the Qurʾān."}, {"id": "96:15/q06/p2", "position": "To blacken, scorch or disfigure by fire or sun.", "reasons": "Al-Māwardī and al-Qurṭubī cite a line about dark hearthstones; al-Khalīl describes a light scorch changing skin color. Al-Ṭabrisī mentions people scorched by fire, and al-Samīn relates marks on a horse, tripods, an angry face, falcons and a dark-cheeked widow. Bint al-Shāṭiʾ says flame and poisonous heat commonly use this verb."}, {"id": "96:15/q06/p3", "position": "To strike or slap the face.", "reasons": "Al-Rāzī reports this gloss; al-Qurṭubī says blows can accompany the seizure and dragging. Bint al-Shāṭiʾ compares a bird smiting its prey with its wings."}, {"id": "96:15/q06/p4", "position": "To brand or mark him.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿAbbās connects Abū Jahl to the branded snout in 68:16; a modern Turkish commentary also records stamping his forehead as a figurative explanation."}, {"id": "96:15/q06/p5", "position": "To humiliate or subjugate him.", "reasons": "Al-Rāzī records this as a separate gloss; ʿAyn al-Maʿānī treats seizure of the forelock as coercion, and modern commentators list disgrace and humiliation among the figurative explanations."}]}
{"id": "96:15/q07", "question": "What event does the forelock threat foretell?", "turns_on": "The notes dispute whether the scene belongs to Judgment, worldly defeat at Badr, or an unspecified act, and whether seizure or scorching is foregrounded.", "positions": [{"id": "96:15/q07/p1", "position": "Abū Jahl will be seized by the forelock and dragged to Hell, especially at the Resurrection.", "reasons": "Al-Farrāʾ, al-Ṭabarī, al-Rāzī and others compare 55:41, where sinners are seized by forelocks and feet. Al-Qurṭubī says he may be folded with his feet and thrown into Hell. Muqātil and Bursevī specify angels dragging him face-first; Ibn Kathīr alternatively allows the forelock to be blackened on Judgment Day. Bint al-Shāṭiʾ hears in the wording both dragging and scorching."}, {"id": "96:15/q07/p2", "position": "He will be seized, restrained and humiliated; the threat may be worldly or unspecified.", "reasons": "Al-Ṭabarī emphasizes restraint and abasement; al-Rāzī explicitly allows this life or the afterlife. {"id": "96:16/q03", "question": "How does the second nāṣiya relate grammatically to the first?", "turns_on": "Which prior expression is supplied as the appositive's antecedent.", "positions": [{"id": "96:16/q03/p1", "position": "It is a genitive appositive or substitute for the preceding forelock.", "reasons": "Sībawayh cites the verse repeatedly for apposition, including his broader examples of noun and appositive and of badal among raised constructions; Ṭabarī says the genitive repeats the previous noun. {"id": "96:16/q11", "question": "Why describe the forelock itself as lying and sinful?", "turns_on": "Whether the transferred qualities exhaust the wording's sense or a literal description remains possible.", "positions": [{"id": "96:16/q11/p1", "position": "The traits belong to its owner and are figuratively assigned to his forelock for a more vivid, forceful threat.", "reasons": "Al-Zajjāj and others compare 'his day fasts and night prays'; Ibn ʿAṭiyya compares a thieving hand; al-Rāzī and Qurṭubī cite faces gazing in 75:23; al-Ālūsī cites 16:62 and the idiom of a face displaying beauty. Al-Zamakhsharī, al-Nasafī, al-Biqāʿī and al-Ālūsī say the transfer intensifies the charge, as though every part sins; Ibn ʿĀshūr pictures the sins visible on the forehead, making it fit for seizure. Al-Biqāʿī adds that the enemy cannot harm the guided person except by God's permission and such harm can elevate the victim. Māwardī, Ṭabrisī, Qurṭubī and Ibn Kathīr specify lying in speech and error in action."}, {"id": "96:16/q11/p2", "position": "The wording may also allow the forelock itself to be described literally.", "reasons": "Elmalılı acknowledges a literal forelock while explaining that the phrase clarifies the intended person."}]}
